A derivative is something that comes from something else. If you take an original thing and build, transform, or develop something new out of it, that new thing is a derivative of the original. It always points back to a source. Without the original, the derivative wouldn't exist or even make sense.

This single core idea runs through every field where the word appears. Once you understand it, all the other uses click into place naturally.

When people use "derivative" casually, they usually mean something unoriginal — something that heavily borrows from a pre-existing source. A film that copies the style and ideas of an older, more original film is called a derivative of it. A new song built on the same chord structure and feel of an older one is a derivative. The word carries a slight negative tone in this context, suggesting the thing lacks originality, because its identity leans too heavily on what came before.

This is the most precise and rigorously defined use of the word, and it is one of the most important ideas in all of mathematics.

The derivative of a function is a measure of how fast that function is changing at any given moment. It captures the instantaneous rate of change.

A simple example: imagine you're on a road trip and tracking your position over time. Your position changes as time passes. The derivative of your position with respect to time gives you your speed — it tells you exactly how fast your position is changing at each instant. If you then take the derivative of your speed, you get your acceleration — how fast your speed itself is changing.

The derivative doesn't just give you an average. It gives you the exact rate of change at a single, specific point — which is why it's so powerful. In practical terms, derivatives are used to find the steepness of a curve at any point, to find the maximum or minimum of a function, and to model how physical systems evolve over time. They sit at the foundation of physics, engineering, economics, and biology.

A financial derivative is a contract whose value is entirely determined by the value of something else — called the "underlying asset." The underlying asset might be a stock, a bond, a commodity (like oil or gold), a currency, or an interest rate.

The crucial point: the derivative itself has no independent value. It is not the asset. It is a contract about the asset. Its worth rises and falls purely because the underlying asset's worth rises and falls.

Common examples include options (the right to buy or sell an asset at a set price before a certain date), futures (an agreement to buy or sell something at a specific future date and price), and swaps (agreements where two parties exchange financial obligations, like fixed vs. variable interest payments).

Financial derivatives are used for two main purposes. Hedging means using them to reduce risk — for example, an airline might use fuel price derivatives to protect itself from sudden spikes in oil prices. Speculation means using them to bet on the future movement of an asset's price in the hopes of making a profit.

Because derivatives can be layered on top of one another and involve enormous sums of money, they can amplify both gains and losses significantly, which makes them both powerful and risky tools in finance.

In chemistry, a derivative is a compound that has been produced from a parent compound through a chemical reaction, while retaining the core structure of the original molecule. Something has been changed — an atom or group of atoms has been added, removed, or substituted — but the fundamental framework remains recognizable.

A classic example: aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is a chemical derivative of salicylic acid. The base molecular structure is preserved, but a small chemical modification was made that changed its properties significantly, making it safer for the stomach while retaining its pain-relieving effect. Morphine and codeine are also derivatives of the same parent compound. The entire field of drug development relies heavily on creating derivatives of known molecules in order to find versions with better effects or fewer side effects.

In the study of language, a derivative is a word that has been formed from another word or root, typically by adding a prefix or a suffix to it. The original word is called the base or root, and the new word derived from it is the derivative.

For example, "happiness" is a derivative of "happy" — formed by adding the suffix "-ness." "Unhappy" is a derivative of "happy" formed by adding the prefix "un-." "Quickly" is a derivative of "quick" formed by adding "-ly." This process of forming new words from existing ones is called derivation, and it is one of the primary ways languages grow and expand their vocabulary.

No matter which domain you are in, a derivative always means the same essential thing: it is downstream from an original source. It is created from, or its meaning/value depends entirely on, something that came before it. The original is the foundation. The derivative is what grows out of that foundation.

A mathematical derivative is derived from a function. A financial derivative is derived from an underlying asset. A chemical derivative is derived from a parent compound. A linguistic derivative is derived from a root word. An everyday derivative is derived from an original creative work.

When you see the word "derivative" used as a noun anywhere, ask yourself: what is this thing derived from? The answer to that question is always the key to understanding what is being described.
